newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - Samsung probe raises Fokker salvage hopes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Samsung probe raises Fokker salvage hopes.

text.p: Bankrupt planemaker Fokker NV said on Friday South Korea's Samsung Aerospace Industries was carrying out exclusive due diligence procedures, raising hopes the company can be salvaged in the coming weeks.

"The focal point of this probe is the question whether all parties involved (among which governments, Stork, banks and the court-appointed receivers) can agree with a business plan currently being finalised by Samsung," Fokker said in a brief statement.
The news marks the most serious approach to the company's heavily loss-making aircraft manufacturing businesses since the group went bankrupt on March 15 this year.
Since then a number of companies have had discussions with Fokker's receivers, notably Aviatsionnaya Korporatsiya Yakovlev of Russia and approaches from three separate Dutch businessmen.
Dutch television reported on Thursday that Samsung was prepared to pay 450 million guilders ($265.5 million) for the bankrupt company and was discussing other conditions with the Dutch government.
The receivers on Friday declined to comment on these figures and said much depended on conditions and contributions from the Dutch and South Korean governments.
The Dutch Economics Ministry said last month that Samsung had requested state support, in return for preserving high-tech jobs in the Netherlands.
The receivers warned against early optimism as Samsung was negotiating with all parties involved, alongside its investigation.
"There are still many issues to address. It's clear that everyone should be nice to each other. It should be lucrative for Samsung, but also for the Netherlands," a spokesman said.

It was the third time that Samsung was in takeover talks at the Fokker headquarters in Amsterdam and the government in The Hague. The two earlier occasions were prior to Fokker's collapse and immediately after it.
Fokker went bankrupt this year after parent company Germany's Daimler Benz Aerospace cut a cash lifeline in January.

The South Korean firm has actively sought to build up a leading role in the aviation industry, but its attempts to do do so at home failed in June when it dropped out of an Asian aircraft building project.

Samsung also needed to come to terms with engineering equipment maker Stork, which took over the profitable maintenance and services arms of Fokker that were saved from the bankruptcy, Fokker Aviation.
Stork has agreed it would sell back these parts of Fokker to a new owner of the planemaking unit if the survival or rebirth of the planemaker depended on it.
But Stork said in August it was involved in the Samsung talks and that selling Fokker Aviation to the South Korean company was not an issue.
Labour unions welcomed the news, but were not ecstatic.
"I'm thrilled to see that talks are more serious than ever before, but I can't be really joyful before I know what it will mean for jobs," said Alex van der Moolen at De Unie.
But he said it was unlikely that Samsung would eventually transfer all jobs to South Korea.
"You can move people to South Korea, but it will be more difficult to build a similar network of suppliers," he said.
